records.name: sweetcorn
records.description: Sweet corn is a cultivar of maize (Zea mays var. saccharata) bred to accumulate higher natural sugar content, harvested young and tender before the kernels mature and starch fully develops. Compared to local field maize, it has a distinctly sweeter, juicier taste with a crisp, tender bite. Popular worldwide, sweet corn is boiled or steamed on the cob, grilled, or used kernel-off-cob in salads, soups, stir-fries, and Indian street snacks like corn chaat. Nutritionally, it offers dietary fiber, carbohydrates, and moderate protein, along with vitamin C, B vitamins (especially folate), magnesium, and antioxidants such as lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health. Its natural sweetness also makes it a favorite in both savory and lightly sweetened preparations.

records.name: swordfish
records.description: Swordfish is a large, fast-swimming ocean fish (Xiphias gladius) known for the long, flat, sword-like bill it uses to slash at prey. As food, it's prized for a few distinct qualities: Texture and flavor: The flesh is firm, meaty, and dense — often compared to a good steak more than to flakier white fish. The flavor is mild but slightly rich, with a subtle sweetness; Cut and cooking: It's usually sold as thick steaks rather than fillets, since the loin is large. It grills, broils, or pan-sears very well, and holds up on skewers (it's a common choice for kebabs); Fat content: It's a moderately fatty fish, which helps keep it moist during high-heat cooking like grilling — unlike very lean white fish that dry out easily.

records.name: sylvaner
records.description: Sylvaner or Silvaner is a variety of white wine grape grown primarily in Alsace and Germany, where its official name is Grüner Silvaner.

records.name: syrah
records.description: Syrah, also known as Shiraz, is a dark-skinned grape variety grown throughout the world and used primarily to produce red wine.

records.name: syrup
records.description: SYRUP is a condiment that is a thick, viscous liquid consisting primarily of a solution of sugar in water, containing a large amount of dissolved sugars but showing little tendency to deposit crystals.

records.name: tahini
records.description: Tahini is a condiment made from toasted ground hulled sesame.

records.name: tahitian taro
records.description: In Hawaii specifically, "Tahitian" is also a distinct named cultivar — it was introduced from Tahiti by horticulturist Gerrit Parmile Wilder.

records.name: taleggio
records.description: TALEGGIO is a semisoft, washed-rind, smear-ripened Italian cheese that is named after Val Taleggio.

records.name: tapioca
records.description: TAPIOCA is a starch extracted from cassava root (tapioca seems to be the same as tapioca starch, but not used as such on ingredient lists)

records.name: taro leaves
records.description: Across the Pacific and Caribbean, taro leaves show up in dishes like callaloo, and in parts of Asia and Africa they're simmered in coconut-based curries or soups. Raw taro leaves are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals, so they need thorough cooking.

records.name: taro shoots
records.description: The young sprouts/suckers that grow off the main corm (sometimes called "huli" in Hawaiian), which are more often used for propagating new plants than eating, though tender young shoots can be cooked too.

records.name: tarragon
records.description: TARRAGON (Artemisia dracunculus), is a species of perennial herb in the sunflower family. Tarragon is one of the four fines herbes of French cooking, and is particularly suitable for chicken, fish, and egg dishes.

records.name: teff
records.description: Teff is a tiny ancient grain native to Ethiopia and Eritrea, where it has been cultivated for thousands of years and remains a dietary staple, most famously as the base for injera flatbread. Despite its small size, it has a rich, slightly sweet, nutty, almost molasses-like flavor. It's typically ground into flour for fermented flatbreads and porridges, or cooked whole as a side grain similar to quinoa. Nutritionally, it's naturally gluten-free and notably high in iron, calcium, and fiber compared to most other grains.

records.name: tequila
records.description: TEQUILA is a regional distilled beverage and type of alcoholic drink made from the blue agave plant, primarily in the area surrounding the city of Tequila

records.name: teran
records.description: Teran grape is a variety of red grape from Istria, Croatia.

records.name: Thai rice
records.description: JASMINE RICE is a long-grain variety of fragrant rice (also known as aromatic rice). Its fragrance, reminiscent of jasmine and popcorn, results from the rice plant's natural production of aromatic compounds

records.name: thistle
records.description: Thistle is the popular name of a group of flowering plants characterised by leaves with sharp spikes on the margins, mostly in the family Asteraceae. (Wikipedia)

records.name: thongweed
records.description: HIMANTHALIA ELONGATA is a brown alga (class Phaeophyta or Phaeophyceae) in the order Fucales, also known by the common names thongweed, sea thong and sea spaghetti.

records.name: thyme
records.description: THYME is an aromatic perennial evergreen herb with culinary, medicinal, and ornamental uses. The most common variety is Thymus vulgaris.

records.name: tilapia
records.description: Tilapia is one of the most widely farmed and eaten fish in the world — a mild, freshwater (or brackish-water) fish that's become a staple in supermarkets and restaurants globally. Flavor and texture: Mild, slightly sweet taste with no strong "fishy" flavor; Firm, flaky white flesh; Because it's so neutral-tasting, it takes on seasonings, marinades, and sauces well — which is a big part of its popularity

records.name: tilefish
records.description: Tilefish is a type of saltwater fish found mainly in the western Atlantic Ocean, from the northeastern U.S. down through the Gulf of Mexico. There are a few species, but the most commonly eaten ones are golden tilefish (also called "white tilefish" in markets) and blueline tilefish. Flavor and texture: Mild, sweet flavor with firm, moist flesh — often compared to a cross between lobster and crab in taste, which is why it's sometimes nicknamed "poor man's lobster." The texture holds up well to various cooking methods. Cooking methods: It works well baked, roasted, pan-seared, grilled, or poached. The skin can be crisped up nicely in a pan. It's popular in Japanese cuisine too, where it's called amadai and often prepared with the scales left on and fried until crispy.

records.name: tilsit
records.description: TILSIT cheese or Tilsiter cheese is a light yellow semihard smear-ripened cheese, created in the mid-19th century by Prussian-Swiss settlers, the Westphal family, from the Emmental valley.

records.name: toasted sesame oil
records.description: “Oil made from toasted seeds is used for its distinctive nutty aroma and taste, although it may be unsuitable for frying, which makes it taste burnt and bitter.” (Wikipedia)

records.name: tofu
records.description: TOFU is a food prepared by coagulating soy milk and then pressing the resulting curds into solid white blocks of varying softness. Tofu has very little flavor or smell of its own. Consequently, tofu can be used in both savory or sweet dishes, acting as a bland background for presenting the flavors of the other ingredients used. In order to flavor the tofu it is often marinated in soy sauce, chillis, sesame oil, etc.

records.name: tomatillo
records.description: Tomatillos are small, round fruits (botanically fruits, culinarily treated as vegetables) that look like little green tomatoes wrapped in a papery husk. They're a staple in Mexican cooking, especially for salsa verde. Tart, tangy, and slightly citrusy — quite different from a regular tomato. Raw ones are firm and sour; cooking mellows and sweetens them a bit.

records.name: tomme
records.description: TOMME, occasionally spelled Tome, is a class of cheese produced mainly in the French Alps and in Switzerland.

records.name: tomme de Savoie
records.description: Tomme de Savoie is an upland variety of Tomme cheese, specifically, one from Savoy in the French Alps.

records.name: tortilla
records.description: A tortilla is a type of thin flatbread, typically made from nixtamalized corn or wheat flour.

records.name: transglutaminase
records.description: In commercial food processing, TRANSGLUTAMINASE is used to bond proteins together. It is produced by Streptoverticillium mobaraense fermentation in commercial quantities or extracted from animal blood.

records.name: tree gum
records.description: sap or other resinous material associated with certain species of the plant kingdom (Wikidata)

records.name: trehalose
records.description: Trehalose is a naturally occurring disaccharide made of two glucose molecules, found in trace amounts in mushrooms, honey, and various plants and insects, and produced commercially today mainly through enzymatic conversion of starch, largely pioneered by Japanese researchers in the 1990s who made large-scale production affordable. It has a mild sweetness—roughly 45% as sweet as sucrose—with no notable aroma, and is valued in food processing for its exceptional stability, ability to protect texture and moisture in frozen or dried foods, and resistance to browning at high heat. Used in baked goods, frozen desserts, and dried fruits as a stabilizer and mild sweetener, trehalose provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, though it's digested more slowly than sucrose, giving it a gentler effect on blood sugar.

records.name: triticale
records.description: Triticale is a hybrid grain bred by crossing wheat and rye, first developed in the late 19th century and refined for commercial use in Europe through the 20th century. Its flour has an earthy, nutty flavor that combines wheat's mildness with rye's slight tanginess. It's used to make breads, pastas, and crackers, often blended with other flours for improved texture and rise. Nutritionally, whole-grain triticale flour is high in fiber, protein, and minerals like magnesium and iron, though it still contains gluten.

records.name: truffle
records.description: A TRUFFLE is the fruiting body of a subterranean ascomycete fungus, predominantly one of the many species of the genus Tuber. In addition to Tuber, many other genera of fungi are classified as truffles including Geopora, Peziza, Choiromyces, Leucangium, and over a hundred others.

records.name: tsunomata
records.description: Tsunomata (角叉, or つのまた) is the Japanese name for a type of red algae/seaweed. In Japanese cooking, it's traditionally soaked and used in salads, soups, or as a crunchy/chewy garnish. It has a mild, subtle sea flavor rather than a strong "seaweed" taste.

records.name: tuber
records.description: A tuber is a swollen underground stem (or in some cases a swollen root), used for storing nutrients — like potatoes. It typically grows at the end of a rhizome or stolon, not as the plant's central root.

records.name: tuna
records.description: A tuna is a saltwater fish that belongs to the tribe Thunnini, a subgrouping of the Scombridae family.

records.name: turkey meat
records.description: TURKEY MEAT, commonly referred to as just turkey, is the meat from turkeys, typically domesticated turkeys. Turkeys are sold sliced and ground, as well as "whole" in a manner similar to chicken with the head, feet, and feathers removed. Frozen whole turkeys remain popular. Sliced turkey is frequently used as a sandwich meat or served as cold cuts.

records.name: turmeric
records.description: TURMERIC is a flowering plant of the ginger family, Zingiberaceae, the roots of which are used in cooking. Note that turmeric contains some curcumine (E100).

records.name: turnip
records.description: The TURNIP (Brassica rapa subsp. rapa) is a root vegetable commonly grown in temperate climates worldwide for its white, fleshy taproot.

records.name: turnip rape
records.description: Turnip rape (Brassica rapa subsp. oleifera, also called field mustard or rybs in some regions) is grown for its seeds, which are pressed for oil. It's one of the plants used to produce canola oil (along with rapeseed, Brassica napus). Young leaves of turnip rape can be eaten as leafy greens, similar to mustard greens or other brassica greens, in some regional cuisines.

records.name: unrefined sea salt from the Atlantic
aliases: unrefined sea salt from the atlantic

records.name: unsalted butter
records.description: All categories of butter are sold in both salted and unsalted forms. Either granular salt or a strong brine are added to salted butter during processing. In addition to enhanced flavor, the addition of salt acts as a preservative.

records.name: vanilla ice cream
records.description: VANILLA ICE CREAM is flavored by artificial or natural vanilla flavoring. The type of vanilla used to flavor ice cream varies by location.

records.name: vanilla sugar
records.description: Vanilla sugar is granulated sugar infused or blended with vanilla flavor—either from real vanilla beans/extract or artificial vanillin—a tradition especially popular in European baking, particularly in Germany, Scandinavia, and Central Europe, where small sachets are a pantry staple. It has a sweet flavor layered with warm, floral, slightly woody vanilla notes, and a texture identical to regular granulated sugar. Commonly stirred into batters, whipped cream, custards, and beverages for a quick flavor boost, vanilla sugar offers no meaningful nutritional value beyond what plain sugar provides—purely empty calories with trace aromatic compounds.

records.name: vanillin
records.description: Vanillin is a phenolic aldehyde, which is an organic compound with the molecular formula C8H8O3.

records.name: vegetable oil
records.description: In common usage, vegetable oil may refer exclusively to vegetable fats which are liquid at room temperature

records.name: vegetable oil and fat
records.description: VEGETABLE OILS, or vegetable fats, are fats extracted from seeds, or less often, from other parts of fruits.

records.name: vegetable oyster
records.description: Root has pale tan or beige skin, with white flesh. Native to the Mediterranean; naturalized widely, including in North America, with the classic "oyster-like" flavor that gave it its common name.

records.name: vermouth
records.description: A dry, or sweet apéritif wine flavored with aromatic herbs, and often used in mixed drinks.

records.name: vine spinach
records.description: Vine spinach (also called Malabar spinach) is a tropical leafy green plant, not a true spinach but used similarly in cooking. It's especially popular in Indian, Filipino, and West African cooking, where it goes by various local names like poi saag (India) or slippery vegetable.

records.name: vinegar
records.description: VINAIGRE is a liquid consisting of about 5–20% acetic acid (CH3COOH), water (H2O), and trace chemicals that may include flavorings.

records.name: vital wheat gluten
records.description: Vital wheat gluten is a concentrated protein extracted from wheat flour by washing away the starch, a process refined industrially in the 20th century to create a versatile baking additive. On its own it's bland and neutral in flavor, though it develops a chewy, meaty texture when hydrated and cooked. It's used to boost elasticity and rise in bread dough, and is a key ingredient in seitan and other plant-based meat substitutes. Nutritionally, it's exceptionally high in protein (over 75%) with very little fat or carbohydrate, though as pure gluten it's unsuitable for those with gluten intolerance or celiac disease.

records.name: wakame
records.description: Wakame (ワカメ), UNDARIA PINNATIFIDA, is a species of edible seaweed, a type of marine algae, and a sea vegetable.

records.name: walnut
records.description: A walnut is the nut of any tree of the genus Juglans. After full ripening for its edible seed when the shell has been discarded, it is used as a garnish or a snack.

records.name: walnut oil
records.description: WALNUT OIL is oil extracted from walnuts, Juglans regia

records.name: wasabi
records.description: WASABI (Eutrema japonicum or Wasabia japonica) or Japanese horseradish is a plant of the Brassicaceae family.

records.name: water
records.description: Water is a naturally occurring compound of hydrogen and oxygen, found throughout the environment in oceans, rivers, lakes, and groundwater, and sourced for consumption from municipal supplies, wells, springs, and glaciers depending on region. It has a neutral, essentially flavorless and odorless profile, though mineral content can lend subtle differences—spring water often tastes slightly mineral-rich, while distilled water tastes notably flat. As the foundation of virtually all food and beverage preparation, water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, though mineral or spring varieties may carry trace amounts of minerals like calcium, magnesium, and potassium, and it remains essential for nearly every bodily function.

records.name: water chestnut
records.description: Eleocharis dulcis, the Chinese water chestnut or water chestnut, is a grass-like sedge. It is grown in many countries for its edible corms.

records.name: water spinach
records.description: Water convolvulus (Ipomoea aquatica), also known as water spinach, morning glory, or kangkong, is a semi-aquatic tropical plant widely used as a leafy vegetable across Asia and Africa. It's a staple vegetable in cuisines across Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia). Both the leaves and tender stem tips are eaten, typically stir-fried with garlic, shrimp paste, or chili.

records.name: Welsh onion
records.description: Allium fistulosum, the Welsh onion, also commonly called bunching onion, long green onion, Japanese bunching onion, and spring onion, is a species of perennial plant. A. fistulosum is an ingredient in Asian cuisine, especially in East and Southeast Asia. In the West, A. fistulosum is primarily used as a scallion or salad onion.

records.name: Wensleydale
records.description: Wensleydale is a style of cheese originally produced in Wensleydale, North Yorkshire, England

records.name: wheat
records.description: WHEAT is a grass widely cultivated for its seed.

records.name: wheat bran fiber
records.description: Wheat bran fiber is derived from the outer layer of the wheat kernel, removed during milling. It has a neutral, slightly nutty taste and a coarse, gritty texture. Widely used across global food industries, it serves as a bulking agent and fiber fortifier in baked goods, cereals, snacks, and pasta, and is also used as a texturizer in processed meats. Nutritionally, it is rich in insoluble dietary fiber, contributing to digestive bulk, along with modest amounts of protein, B vitamins, and minerals like magnesium and iron. Its low fat and calorie content make it valued as a functional, fiber-dense ingredient worldwide.

records.name: wheat flour
records.description: Wheat flour comes from wheat, one of the world's oldest cultivated grains, first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent around 10,000 years ago and now the dominant grain in global bread-making, especially in Europe, the Middle East, and the Americas. It has a mild, slightly sweet, neutral flavor with a texture that ranges from soft and fine (cake flour) to coarse and hearty (whole wheat), largely defined by its protein and gluten content, which gives dough its characteristic elasticity and chew. Wheat flour contains gluten and, depending on whether it's whole grain or refined, provides varying levels of fiber, B vitamins, iron, and protein—whole wheat retaining significantly more nutrients since the bran and germ aren't stripped away.

records.name: wheat germ
records.description: WHEAT GERM is a concentrated source of several essential nutrients, including vitamin E, folate (folic acid), phosphorus, thiamin, zinc, and magnesium, as well as essential fatty acids and fatty alcohols. It is a good source of fiber. Wheat germ can be added to protein shakes, casseroles, muffins, pancakes, cereals, yogurt, smoothies, cookies, and other goods.

records.name: wheat semolina
records.description: Suji (semolina) is a coarsely milled wheat product, made by grinding the hard endosperm of wheat (often durum wheat) into granular particles, with bran and germ largely removed — similar refinement to maida but coarser in texture. Used across the Mediterranean and South Asia for centuries, it has a mild, slightly nutty taste and a distinctive grainy, granular texture that gives dishes a light, fluffy bite. Used for upma, sheera/halwa, dosa batter, idli, pasta, and as a coating for frying. Nutritionally, it's calorie-dense with moderate protein, but low in fiber like maida, retaining few micronutrients from the removed bran and germ.

records.name: wheat vermicelli
records.description: Vermicelli (seviyan) is a thin, thread-like noodle made by extruding wheat dough — typically from refined flour or semolina — through fine dies, then drying (and often lightly roasting). Popular across South Asia and the Middle East, it has a mild, neutral-to-toasty taste depending on roasting, with a delicate, springy texture once cooked. Used in sweet dishes like seviyan kheer, and savory preparations like vermicelli upma. Nutritionally, it resembles maida — calorie-dense, low in fiber and micronutrients — though roasting doesn't significantly change its core nutrient profile.

records.name: whey
records.description: WHEY is the liquid remaining after milk has been curdled and strained.

records.name: whey protein
records.description: WHEY PROTEIN is a mixture of globular proteins isolated from whey, the liquid material created as a by-product of cheese production.

records.name: whipping cream
records.description: Whipping cream is a high-fat dairy product (typically 30–36% milk fat) that, when chilled and beaten, traps air to form soft or stiff peaks. It is lightly sweetened for desserts, holds its shape for piping, and adds a rich, velvety mouthfeel to mousses, ganaches, and sauces. Because of its lower fat content than heavy cream, it whips faster but is less stable over time.

records.name: white brugnon
records.description: Native to China, brugnons spread along ancient trade routes into Persia and the Mediterranean, where Mediterranean climates now support major cultivation. The white-fleshed variety offers a delicate, low-acid sweetness compared to yellow varieties, with smooth, fuzz-free skin and flesh that clings to the pit. Consumed fresh as a snack or dessert fruit, it also features in salads, tarts, and preserves across various cuisines. Nutritionally, it provides vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber, along with natural sugars and antioxidant compounds, making it a commonly consumed seasonal stone fruit in temperate regions worldwide.

records.name: white chocolate
records.description: WHITE CHOCOLATE is made of sugar, milk, and cocoa butter, without the cocoa solids. It is pale ivory colour, and lacks many of the compounds found in milk and dark chocolates.

records.name: white corn
records.description: White corn is from the whole kernel of white corn — a corn variety that lacks the yellow/orange carotenoid pigments found in standard yellow corn. it's very similar to whole-grain yellow corn flour in calories, protein, and fiber — the main practical difference is the near-absence of vitamin A precursors.

records.name: white icicle radish
records.description: White Icicle radish is a heirloom radish variety, notable for its long, slender white root. Milder and less peppery-hot than round red radishes, with a crisp, juicy bite.

records.name: white lentil
records.description: Hulled and split black gram. Hulling removes the black skin which gives it a white color.

records.name: white soybean
records.description: White soybeans, more accurately pale yellow in color, are the most widely cultivated variety of soybean (Glycine max), grown extensively across the Americas, East Asia, and other major agricultural regions worldwide. They have a mild, neutral flavor, making them highly versatile in food production. This variety forms the basis of most global soy products, including tofu, soy milk, soybean oil, tempeh, and edamame. As the dominant type in commercial and everyday use, white soybeans are valued nutritionally for their high plant protein content, dietary fiber, and essential fatty acids.

records.name: white walnut
records.description: Butternuts (Juglans cinerea), also called white walnuts, are a species of walnut tree native to eastern North America. The nutmeats are eaten and used in baking.

records.name: white whole grain corn flour
records.description: White corn flour is a flour ground from the whole kernel of white corn — a corn variety that lacks the yellow/orange carotenoid pigments found in standard yellow corn. it's very similar to whole-grain yellow corn flour in calories, protein, and fiber — the main practical difference is the near-absence of vitamin A precursors.

records.name: white wine
records.description: WHITE WINE is a wine whose colour can be straw-yellow, yellow-green, or yellow-gold.

records.name: white-flowered gourd
records.description: "White-flowered gourd" (calabash) refers to Lagenaria siceraria — also known as bottle gourd, calabash gourd, opo squash, or long melon. It's the same plant whose hard-shelled fruits are dried and used as bottles, bowls, or musical instruments, but when eaten as food it's harvested young and tender, before the shell hardens. Very mild, slightly sweet, with a texture similar to zucchini or chayote — it takes on the flavor of whatever it's cooked with. Common in cuisines: South Asian (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh — called lauki, doodhi, or ghiya), Chinese (hu lu), Vietnamese, Italian (cucuzza), and West African cooking. One caution worth knowing: bottle gourds can occasionally develop high levels of cucurbitacins (the compound that makes some gourds bitter), which can cause food poisoning. The rule of thumb is — if it tastes bitter, don't eat it, even if just one bite.

records.name: whiteleg shrimp
records.description: Whiteleg shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei, formerly Penaeus vannamei), also known as Pacific white shrimp or king prawn, is a variety of prawn of the eastern Pacific Ocean commonly caught or farmed for food.

records.name: whole rye and durum wheat sourdough
aliases: whole rye and durum wheat sourdough

records.name: whole wheat kernels
records.description: Whole wheat grain (Triticum aestivum) is the raw, unprocessed wheat kernel — bran, germ, and endosperm all intact, unmilled. Cultivated for over 8,000 years since its Fertile Crescent origins, it's the source grain from which both atta and maida are later produced. Raw, it has a hard, chewy texture with an earthy, nutty taste; when cracked (dalia) or sprouted, it becomes softer and slightly sweet. Used for porridge, khichdi, upma, sprouted salads, or ground fresh into atta. Nutritionally, it's the most nutrient-dense wheat form — highest in fiber, iron, zinc, magnesium, and B-vitamins, since nothing has been removed.

records.name: whole-grain blue corn flour
records.description: Blue corn flour is a stone-ground flour made from whole kernels of blue (or purple) corn — a corn variety, distinct from standard yellow or white corn, that owes its color to natural anthocyanin pigments (the same class of antioxidant compounds found in blueberries and purple cabbage). it's generally comparable to other whole-grain corn flours in calories and carbohydrates, but the anthocyanin content gives it additional antioxidant properties and a naturally sweeter, nuttier flavor than yellow corn flour.

records.name: wine
records.description: WINE is an alcoholic beverage made from fermented grapes.

records.name: winged beans
records.description: Winged beans (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus) are a tropical legume known for their distinctive four-sided, ruffled or "winged" pods — the edges look like jagged ribbons running down the length of each pod. Almost the entire plant is edible: pods, seeds, leaves, flowers, and even the tuberous roots can all be eaten. That's unusual among legumes. High in protein: the seeds in particular are very protein- and nutrient-dense, which is part of why they've been studied as a potential "supercrop" for tropical regions. Native to Southeast Asia and New Guinea, and widely grown across South and Southeast Asia, as well as parts of Africa.

records.name: wood ear
records.description: "Cloud ear" (also called wood ear, black fungus, or mù'ěr 木耳 in Chinese) refers to mushrooms in the genus Auricularia — most commonly Auricularia auricula-judae or Auricularia cornea. They're a type of jelly fungus that grows on decaying or living wood, especially elder, beech, and other broadleaf trees. Cloud ears are prized more for their texture than flavor — they're crunchy, slightly gelatinous, and almost cartilaginous when cooked, but have very little taste of their own. That makes them great at soaking up other flavors in a dish.

records.name: worcestershire sauce
records.description: WORCESTERSHIRE SAUCE is a fermented liquid condiment created in the city of Worcester. Worcestershire sauce is frequently used to enhance food and drink recipes.

records.name: wort
records.description: Liquid extracted from the mashing process during brewing.

records.name: xylanase
records.description: Xylanase is any of a class of enzymes that degrade the linear polysaccharide xylan into xylose,[1] thus breaking down hemicellulose, one of the major components of plant cell walls.

records.name: yam
records.description: Yam is the common name for some plant species in the genus Dioscorea (family Dioscoreaceae) that form edible tubers. In some places, other (unrelated) root vegetables are sometimes referred to as "yams".

records.name: yambean
records.description: Yambean is a tropical legume (in the bean family, Fabaceae) grown primarily for its large, starchy, edible tuber/root. Native to Mexico and Central America, widely cultivated across Latin America and Southeast Asia. Mildly sweet, very crunchy, similar to a cross between an apple and a water chestnut — it stays crisp even when cooked.

records.name: yardlong beans
records.description: Yardlong beans (also called Chinese long beans, snake beans, or asparagus beans) are a type of legume known for their dramatically long, slender pods — typically 12 to 30 inches long, though they're usually picked and sold around 18 inches. They have a slightly nuttier, more savory flavor than regular green beans, with a denser, chewier texture that holds up well to high-heat cooking like stir-frying. They're a staple in Chinese, Southeast Asian (especially Thai, Vietnamese, Filipino), and South Asian cooking.

records.name: yautia
records.description: Yautia (also called malanga or taro coco) is a starchy root vegetable widely used in Latin American and Caribbean cuisine. Earthy, slightly nutty flavor, denser and less slimy than taro. When cooked, it becomes soft and starchy — similar to a potato but with more depth of flavor.

records.name: yeast
records.description: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, most commonly Saccharomyces cerevisiae, used for thousands of years since ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian times to leaven bread and ferment beverages like beer and wine, long before its microbial nature was understood. It has a mild, slightly savory, umami flavor with a subtly yeasty, bread-like aroma, and comes in fresh, active dry, or instant forms that vary in texture from soft and crumbly to fine granules. Used in baking, brewing, and winemaking, yeast works by converting sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol through fermentation, and nutritional yeast (a deactivated form) is notably rich in B vitamins, protein, and often fortified with B12, making it a popular supplement for plant-based diets.

records.name: yeast extract
records.description: Yeast extract is a savory paste or powder made by breaking down yeast cells—typically through autolysis (self-digestion using the yeast's own enzymes) or hydrolysis—a byproduct process refined in the late 19th century that led to iconic products like Marmite in the UK and Vegemite in Australia. It has an intensely savory, salty, umami-rich flavor with deep, almost meaty notes, and comes as a thick, sticky spread or dried into a fine powder used as a seasoning. Used as a flavor enhancer in soups, sauces, stocks, and spreads, yeast extract is naturally rich in glutamic acid (contributing its umami punch), B vitamins, and protein, making it both a flavor booster and a modest nutritional contributor.

records.name: yellow corn
records.description: Yellow corn is from the whole kernel of yellow corn, the most common corn type used in the US. Yellow corn gets its color from carotenoids, including beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A — so unlike white corn flour, yellow corn flour has some vitamin A activity.

records.name: yellow mung dal
records.description: Hulled and split mung bean

records.name: yellow whole-grain corn flour
records.description: Yellow corn flour is flour ground from the whole kernel of yellow corn, the most common corn type used in the US. Yellow corn gets its color from carotenoids, including beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A — so unlike white corn flour, yellow corn flour has some vitamin A activity.

records.name: yellowfin tuna
records.description: The yellowfin tuna (Thunnus albacares) is a species of tuna found in pelagic waters of tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide.
